content.title: Stop Splitting Your Repos Before You Have a Reason To
content.text:
Every few months a team I advise asks whether it should break its codebase into separate repositories. The question usually arrives right after a painful week: a flaky build, a dependency upgrade that touched forty packages, or a new hire who could not find anything. Splitting feels like hygiene. For most teams under about two hundred engineers, I think it is the wrong default, and the evidence I have seen points the same way.

Start with the cost that motivates the split: build time. The fear is that one repository means one enormous build. In practice modern build tooling makes this a non-issue at the scale we are talking about. The 2025 Ridgeline Software internal report, which tracked 31 product teams over eighteen months, found that median CI time for teams on a single repository with content-addressed caching was 6.4 minutes, against 5.9 minutes for teams on a polyrepo layout. That half-minute is real but it is not the difference anyone is imagining when they picture a monolith compiling for an hour. And the monorepo teams paid for it once, at the pipeline level, while the polyrepo teams paid every time someone set up a new repository with its own slightly different configuration.

The larger cost hides in changes that span more than one service. In the same Ridgeline data, 38 percent of changes on polyrepo teams touched at least two repositories. Those changes took a median of 3.2 days from first commit to full deployment, compared with 0.9 days for equivalent changes on monorepo teams. The gap was not review time; it was coordination: opening pull requests in the right order, waiting for a published package version, bumping a lockfile, discovering the bump broke a consumer that nobody had checked. A survey of 412 engineers by the Cartwright Institute for Software Practice in early 2026 asked respondents to name their single most common source of a wasted day, and cross-repository version coordination came second, behind only environment setup.

There is also a quieter effect on quality. When a shared library lives in its own repository, its authors cannot see who depends on what. Hana Okoro, who led platform engineering at a 140-person payments company she has written about under the name Fennelbrook, described upgrading an internal HTTP client across nineteen repositories. Eleven of them had pinned a version two years old. Three had forked the client and never merged back. In a monorepo, she noted, the same upgrade would have been one change with a compiler telling her exactly which call sites broke. Her team's incident log over the following year attributed four production incidents to version skew between services that were supposed to be running the same library.

I want to be fair to the polyrepo case, because it is not empty. Access control is genuinely harder in a single repository; if you have a compliance boundary that says some engineers must not see some code, splitting is the simplest way to enforce it. Repository size can also become a problem for the tooling, and the Ridgeline report notes that two teams with large binary assets checked in saw clone times of over ten minutes before they adopted partial clones. And ownership can blur. When everything is in one place, it is easy for a team to edit code it does not own without talking to anyone, and some organisations prefer the friction of a separate repository as a forcing function for conversation.

Those are real trade-offs. My claim is only that they are trade-offs a team should reach deliberately, after feeling the pain, rather than adopt as a default. Below roughly two hundred engineers, the coordination costs of many repositories arrive early and reliably, while the scaling costs of one repository arrive late and can be handled with tooling that already exists. If you are going to make a mistake, make the one that is cheap to reverse. Merging repositories after years of drift is a project; splitting a well-structured monorepo along a module boundary is an afternoon.

So my advice to the team asking the question is usually the same. Fix the build cache, write down who owns which directory, and keep everything together until a specific, measured problem tells you otherwise.

notes: Measured opinion piece arguing monorepos are the right default for teams under ~200 engineers, with specific fictional build-time and cross-repo change data and explicit concessions. A correct judge should recognise it as substantive, evidence-backed argument rather than hot-take or rage-bait.
